abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
               <jats:p>Norbert Lohfink (1928–2024) was one of the most influential figures in Catholic biblical scholarship after the Second Vatican Council. His courageous and innovative theories have inspired generations of biblical scholars and provoked lively discussions far beyond the boundaries of the subject. He dealt with fundamental questions of biblical hermeneutics that are still relevant today. Particular mention should be made of his studies on Deuteronomy, the Deuteronomistic History, Ecclesiastes and the Psalms.</jats:p>
title: Katholische Bibelwissenschaft nach dem II. Vaticanum – Norbert Lohfink in memoriam (1928–2024)

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
               <jats:p>The debate surrounding the composition of the Book of Ezekiel has reached a stalemate, with the scholarly discourse relying on the limited evidence provided by the biblical text. The present article introduces new insights from Persian-period Mesopotamian sources, which illuminate the historical and geographical context of several passages in the book. These findings contribute to a deeper understanding of its literary formation.</jats:p>
title: The Composition of the Book of Ezekiel in Light of Babylonian Sources

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
               <jats:p>This article suggests that Prov 9 serves as an introduction to Prov 10:1–22:16, »dramatizing« it as competing banquets of Wisdom and Folly. Proverbial knowledge allows to discern between the invitations of the two voices. It enables the student of wisdom to navigate a life amidst ambiguities and uncanniness. Proverbial thinking teaches a phenomenological and critical hermeneutics that takes response-ability––i.e. the ability to respond––seriously. The uneducated person (<jats:named-content content-type="rtl" specific-use="bidi">פְּתִי</jats:named-content>) must learn to which call they should respond. Folly/chaos is therefore an integral part of Wisdom/order.</jats:p>
title: Uncanny Resemblances – Prov 9 as an Introduction to Proverbial Thinking

<jats:title>Résumé</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>L’exégèse historico-critique contemporaine peine à trouver un consensus interprétatif sur le sens de la clôture du deutéro-Isaïe, soit Isaïe 55,12–13. Cette étude propose d’aborder le sujet via un angle nouveau, en partant des plantes mentionnées dans la prophétie. En conjuguant une analyse littéraire des différents végétaux présents dans le texte et des contextes historiques qu’ils peuvent évoquer à la lumière des sources anciennes et des travaux modernes de paléobotanique, une nouvelle lecture en lien avec le contexte d’un discours enthousiaste sur le Second Temple à l’époque tardo-perse ou au début de l’époque hellénistique est proposée.</jats:p>
title: Isaïe 55,12–13 : Une enquête botanique et littéraire sur la clôture du deutéro-Isaïe

                  <jats:p>
                    Interpretations of the Hebrew lexeme
                    <jats:named-content content-type="rtl" specific-use="bidi">צלמות</jats:named-content>
                    often revolve around the question whether it denotes an abstract noun (»darkness«) or a compound (»shadow of death«). We propose that the Septuagint played a key role in the development of the Masoretic reading of
                    <jats:named-content content-type="rtl" specific-use="bidi">צלמות</jats:named-content>
                    as
                    <jats:named-content content-type="rtl" specific-use="bidi">צַלְמָוֶת</jats:named-content>
                    . The frequent use of compounds in ancient Greek and the centrality of compounds in Greek etymology likely influenced the Septuagint’s reading of
                    <jats:named-content content-type="rtl" specific-use="bidi">צלמות</jats:named-content>
                    as a compound. This etymological interpretation became embedded in Greek-Jewish discourse and contributed to the development of the Masoretic interpretation
                    <jats:named-content content-type="rtl" specific-use="bidi">צַלְמָוֶת</jats:named-content>
                    .
                  </jats:p>
title: The Contribution of the Septuagint to the Masoretic Reading of צלמות

               <jats:p>In diesem Artikel wird argumentiert, dass der hebräische Text von Genesis 7,20 anders zu verstehen ist als bisher angenommen wurde. Der adverbiale Ausdruck <jats:italic>mil<jats:sup>e</jats:sup>maˁlā<jats:sup>h</jats:sup>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    The enigmatic Hebrew term
                    <jats:italic>›vehutzav‹</jats:italic>
                    has sparked intense debate among Bible translators and scholars for centuries. Is it a name, a divine command, or a reference to a queen’s demise? Ancient texts provide no definitive answers, and contemporary English translations vary significantly, ranging from the mysterious ›Huzzab‹ to the foreboding ›it is decreed‹. With at least seven differing interpretations available, this single word has the potential to alter our comprehension of Nahum’s prophecy regarding Nineveh. This research delves into the core of this enigma, employing textual criticism as its methodology to untangle one of the Old Testament’s most persistent linguistic challenges and clarify Nahum’s true message about Nineveh’s destiny.
                  </jats:p>
title: Cracking the Mystery of the Hebrew Word › vehutzav ‹

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
               <jats:p>The recent study by Nadav Naʾaman on the Judean »fiscal« bullae from private collections supports the reliability of the synchronism between the deaths of Ahaz and Tiglath-pileser III in Isa 14:28–29. Close attention to this synchronism and to the way it is anchored in Mesopotamian chronology dates the death of Ahaz and the enthronement of Hezekiah to 727/6 BCE (a year later than suggested by Naʾaman) and leads to important conclusions concerning the calendars and the systems of counting regnal years practiced in the courts of Hezekiah of Judah and his contemporary, Hoshea of Israel.</jats:p>
title: Chronological Notes on the Reigns of Hezekiah and Hoshea

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
               <jats:p>The so-called blessings of Jacob in Gen 49 are full of textual and interpretive difficulties. The concentration of these difficulties in the verses concerning Judah (Gen 49:8–12) and Joseph (Gen 49:22–26) points to their origin in conflict over the locus of legitimate kingship. This article argues that a number of these problems are a result of disputes between the descendants of those deported to Babylon with Jehoiachin in 597 BCE and the descendants of those left behind with Zedekiah in the homeland. The high concentration of textual problems in Gen 49 is consistent with similar textual difficulties in other texts concerned with this conflict.</jats:p>
title: Contested Kingship: Joseph, Jehoiachin, and Judah in Genesis 49

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Redaction critics have dated the doxologies in Daniel 4–6 based on the theme of God’s eternal kingdom, which they share with Psalm 145. This article attempts to show that there are many other linguistic features and theological assertions shared by the doxologies in Daniel 2–6 and Psalm 145, as well as the doxologies in Jeremiah 10:1–16, which might be relevant to dating the composition of the doxologies in Daniel 2–6. Their occurrence in the apocalyptic vision in Daniel 7 suggests that the author/redactors of Daniel 7 might be responsible for the doxologies in Daniel.</jats:p>
title: The Relevance of Psalm 145 and Jeremiah 10:1–16 to the Dating of the Doxologies in Daniel 2–6

abstract:
<jats:title>Zusammenfassung</jats:title>
               <jats:p>Die Eröffnung des Sacharjabuches in Sach 1,1–6 ist weniger eine Bußpredigt als vielmehr der Entwurf einer Theologie der alttestamentlichen Prophetie insgesamt. Die vorexilischen Propheten werden hier innovativ als die »früheren Propheten« bezeichnet. Deren Botschaft war demnach der Ruf »Kehrt um!«. Die damit verbundenen Drohungen sind eingetroffen, was wiederum ein Erweis für die Verlässlichkeit des Wortes Gottes für die zeitgenössische Leserschaft ist. So ist Sach 1,1–6 ein theologischer Programmtext, der für ein bestimmtes Bild der Prophetie Begriffe sucht und findet.</jats:p>
title: Die Eröffnung des Sacharjabuches (Sach 1,1–6) als prophetentheologischer Programmtext

               <jats:p>Die Bücher Joel und Jona weisen zwei markante intertextuelle Bezüge auf: Joel 2,13; Jona 4,2 bieten eine einmalige Version der Gnadenformel, bei der Gottes Reue (<jats:named-content content-type="rtl" specific-use="bidi">נחם</jats:named-content>) an die Stelle seiner Treue (<jats:named-content content-type="rtl" specific-use="bidi">אמת</jats:named-content>) tritt, und in Joel 2,14; Jona 3,9 stimmt die Wendung <jats:named-content content-type="rtl" specific-use="bidi">מי־יודע ישׁוב ונחם</jats:named-content> überein. Der Beitrag stellt die Mehrheitsposition, dass Jona Joel zitiere, infrage. Er legt erstens dar, dass der literarische Befund an diesen Stellen für die Priorität Jonas spricht, und zeigt zweitens auf, wie und mit welcher Aussageabsicht das Buch Jona seine Aussagen zu Gottes Reue geformt und Joel sie von dort übernommen hat.</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
               <jats:p>In prophetic texts, humor is frequently employed to mock the hubris of imperial powers and rulers. This article describes various forms and stylistic devices of mockery such as caricaturing exaggerations, irony, alienation of genres, the grotesque, and mythical coloring, thereby working out the subversive function of »humor from below«. This type of humor serves to critique power and to expose and shame the (once) powerful. In 2Kgs 19:21 par. Isa 37:22, this mockery of imperial hubris is even personally embodied by daughter Zion.</jats:p>
title: Subversive Humor and the Critique of Imperial Hubris in Prophetic Texts

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
               <jats:p>Three orders of legal collections can be identified conceptually in the Pentateuch: <jats:italic>hattôrāh</jats:italic>, <jats:italic>hāʽedut</jats:italic> and <jats:italic>hammiṣwāh</jats:italic>. A comparison of their Greek textual and Masoretic vocalisation traditions can identify linguistic impulses that subordinate <jats:italic>hāʽedut</jats:italic> and <jats:italic>hammiṣwāh</jats:italic> to the legal system of the Dtn. <jats:italic>hattôrāh</jats:italic>. This article details why, in the Hellenistic period, <jats:italic>hattôrāh</jats:italic> could have emerged from a reframing of the pre-existing <jats:italic>hammiṣwāh</jats:italic>, which other textual witnesses confirm is older than <jats:italic>hattôrāh</jats:italic>.</jats:p>
title: hammiṣwāh  – a Forgotten Forerunner of the Deuteronomic Torah?

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
               <jats:p>The hapax legomenon <jats:named-content content-type="rtl" specific-use="bidi">פַּנַּג</jats:named-content>
                  <jats:italic>pannag</jats:italic> is mentioned in Ezekiel as an export of the land of Israel to the international market in Tyre (Ezek 27:17). It has been interpreted in wildly different ways, with the dominant view now being that it is a kind of baked good or flour. A few scholars have noted Greek πάνακες »allheal« as an apparent cognate, but they have not realized its significance. It is argued here that Hebrew <jats:italic>pannag</jats:italic> and its Akkadian cognate <jats:italic>pinigu</jats:italic> both derive from Greek πάνακες and denote a medicinal product of the <jats:italic>Ferula</jats:italic> (giant fennel) plant or of a related genus. Accordingly, <jats:italic>pannag</jats:italic> should be translated »allheal.«</jats:p>
title: Identifying Pannag, an Ancient Product of Israel

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
               <jats:p>This essay explores the significance of the Sabbath’s inclusion in Leviticus 23 by analyzing the expressions <jats:named-content content-type="rtl" specific-use="bidi">שבת שבתון</jats:named-content>, <jats:named-content content-type="rtl" specific-use="bidi">שבתון</jats:named-content>, and <jats:named-content content-type="rtl" specific-use="bidi">שבע שבת</jats:named-content>[<jats:named-content content-type="rtl" specific-use="bidi">ו</jats:named-content>]<jats:named-content content-type="rtl" specific-use="bidi">ת</jats:named-content>. It uncovers a framework linking the Sabbath, Day of Atonement, and Sabbatical Year, highlighting the Sabbath’s central role. This study investigates the seventh-month festivals and examines the social justice implications of the Sabbatical Year, Jubilee, and grain harvest festival, all structured around the Sabbath concept. The findings indicate that H’s sabbatical framework marks a significant development in the conceptualization of sacred time.</jats:p>
title: Sabbatical Framework of Sacred Times in H

abstract:
<jats:title>Résumé</jats:title>
               <jats:p>S’inspirant de l’étude classique de V.J. Propp <jats:italic>Morphologie du conte</jats:italic>, l’article décrit la morphologie abstraite des courts récits miraculeux sur Élisée dans 2 Rois, et procède ensuite à une analyse plus détaillée de certaines de leurs caractéristiques particulières. Malgré leur couleur populaire, ces légendes sont profondément marquées par l’image de la prophétie qui s’est imposée parmi les lettrés judéens aux époques exilique et perse. Il semble donc que ces textes n’aient pas seulement été insérés dans les Rois à l’époque postexilique, mais qu’ils aient aussi été composés à cette époque, même s’ils peuvent contenir quelques motifs anciens.</jats:p>
title: Forme et fonction de courts récits miraculeux sur Élisée
